**Astra is a command-line contact book for people who network a lot.** Capture each new person you meet (name, company, role, phone, email and LinkedIn) in the seconds between conversations, then pull them up again before you next meet.
* **Who it is for:** students and professionals who attend networking events, career fairs and conferences, type fast, and are comfortable with a CLI.
* `add` a contact with their name, and optionally a company, role, phone number, email, LinkedIn profile and tags
* `find` a contact by part of their name, or by phone number or email, and `view` everything stored about them
* `edit` details that were mistyped or have changed, one field or several at a time
* `delete` a contact by name or by its number in the list, or `clear` the whole list
* `list` all contacts, `help` for command formats, and `exit`
* Refuses to store two contacts under the same name, or to give one contact a phone number or email already saved for another, whether you are adding or editing
* Saves automatically after every change, and recovers what it can from a corrupted data file
* **Planned for after the MVP:** several companies, roles, numbers or emails per contact; deleting by
email or phone number; deleting several contacts at once; a confirmation prompt before `delete` and
`clear`; merging duplicate records rather than only refusing them; and treating names that differ
only in letter case as the same contact.

This project uses Gradle for **build automation and dependency management**. **We recommend reading [this Gradle tutorial from se-edu/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/gradle.html).**
The following commands perform common Gradle tasks.
* **`clean`**: Deletes the files created during the previous build tasks (e.g. files in the `build` folder).
* **`shadowJar`**: Uses the Shadow plugin to create the fat JAR file `build/libs/contactfile.jar`.
**`runShadow`**: Builds the application as a fat JAR, then runs it.
* **`checkstyleMain`**: Runs the code style check for the main code base.
**`checkstyleTest`**: Runs the code style check for the test code base.
* `./gradlew clean test`: Cleans the project before running all tests
This project uses GitHub Actions for CI. The necessary workflow configuration files are in `.github/workflows`. No further setup is required.
As part of CI, Gradle generates JaCoCo coverage reports from the tests, and CI uploads the coverage data to Codecov. Codecov then provides information about test coverage.

However, because Codecov is known to run into intermittent problems (e.g., report upload fails) due to issues on the Codecov service side, the CI is configured to pass even if the Codecov task failed. Therefore, developers are advised to check the code coverage levels periodically and take corrective actions if the coverage level falls below desired levels.
To enable Codecov for forks of this project, follow the steps given in [this se-edu guide](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/codecov.html).

* Checks are implemented as executable `check-*` scripts within the `.github` directory. The `run-checks.sh` script will automatically pick up and run files named as such. That is, you can add more such files if you need and the CI will do the rest.
* Check scripts should print out errors in the format `SEVERITY:FILENAME:LINE: MESSAGE`
* SEVERITY is either ERROR or WARN.
* FILENAME is the path to the file relative to the current directory.
* LINE is the line of the file where the error occurred and MESSAGE is the message explaining the error.
* Check scripts must exit with a non-zero exit code if any errors occur.

The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F13-2/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F13-2/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.

* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other. It loads the saved contacts through `Storage` before creating `Model`, so that any recovery done at startup can be reported by `UI`.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
In the diagram, a solid arrow means the component holds a reference to the other one, and a dashed arrow means it only
depends on it. `UI` keeps a reference to `Logic` and shows data from `Model`, but never changes `Model` itself: every
user command goes through `Logic`, which updates `Model` and asks `Storage` to save the changes. `UI` depends on
`Storage` only for the startup result it displays (whether the contacts were loaded or recovered), and
`Storage` depends on `Model` for the data it reads and writes.

* stores the contact file data i.e., all `Person` objects, in a `UniquePersonList` inside a `ContactFile`. `ModelManager` builds its own copies of the `ContactFile` and `UserPrefs` it is given, so it owns them (composition).

* a `Person` always has a `Name`, and may additionally have a `Company`, `Role`, `Phone`, `Email`, `Linkedin` and an introducer (the `Name` of the person who introduced them). Every field other than the name is optional, because a contact met at a networking event is often captured with only the details that were exchanged. Optional fields are exposed as `Optional<...>` so callers must handle an absent value. These single-value classes, and `Tag`, are shown as attributes of `Person` rather than as separate classes.
* a `Person` also holds any number of tags, `Event`s, `FollowUp`s and `Interaction`s, a starred flag, and the last follow-up ID it allocated.

* `Person` is immutable. `withStarred`, `withEvent`, `appendFollowUp`, `removeFollowUp` and `withInteraction` each return a new `Person`, which `Model#setPerson` puts in place of the old one. The new `Person` shares its unchanged `Event`, `FollowUp` and `Interaction` objects with the old one, so these are drawn as associations rather than compositions.
* `Person#isSamePerson` compares equal names and emails that are either both absent or equal ignoring case.
Current add/edit validation separately rejects shared normalized phone numbers and case-insensitive emails.
Follow-ups, retired action IDs, events, interactions, and starred status do not change contact identity.

* a `FollowUp` has an ID, a description, an optional due date and a `Status` (`PENDING` or `COMPLETED`). `FollowUp#isOverdue` is true for a pending follow-up whose due date has passed. `Model#getFollowUps` creates a `FollowUpEntry` for each follow-up, pairing it with its contact; `Model#getPendingFollowUps` retains only pending actions from that snapshot.

* stores the `Person` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list (`filteredPersons`). It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.

* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (GUI settings, command aliases and the global contact field order). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object. The field order is a `FieldOrder`, which lists each of the nine `Field` values exactly once.

file. Failed writes, invalid/different/missing candidates, or replacement

`ContactFileParser` keeps the only list of built-in command words. `ContactFileParser#expandShortcut` replaces a

The proposed undo/redo mechanism is facilitated by `VersionedContactFile`. It extends `ContactFile` with an undo/redo history, stored internally as a `contactFileStateList` and `currentStatePointer`. Additionally, it implements the following operations:
* `VersionedContactFile#commit()` — Saves the current contact file state in its history.
* `VersionedContactFile#undo()` — Restores the previous contact file state from its history.
* `VersionedContactFile#redo()` — Restores a previously undone contact file state from its history.
These operations are exposed in the `Model` interface as `Model#commitContactFile()`, `Model#undoContactFile()` and `Model#redoContactFile()` respectively.
Given below is an example usage scenario and how the undo/redo mechanism behaves at each step.

Step 1. The user launches the application for the first time. The `VersionedContactFile` will be initialized with the initial contact file state, and the `currentStatePointer` pointing to that single contact file state.

Step 2. The user executes `delete 5` command to delete the 5th person in the contact file. The `delete` command calls `Model#commitContactFile()`, causing the modified state of the contact file after the `delete 5` command executes to be saved in the `contactFileStateList`, and the `currentStatePointer` is shifted to the newly inserted contact file state.

Step 3. The user executes `add n/David …​` to add a new person. The `add` command also calls `Model#commitContactFile()`, causing another modified contact file state to be saved into the `contactFileStateList`.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If a command fails its execution, it will not call `Model#commitContactFile()`, so the contact file state will not be saved into the `contactFileStateList`.

Step 4. The user now decides that adding the person was a mistake, and decides to undo that action by executing the `undo` command. The `undo` command will call `Model#undoContactFile()`, which will shift the `currentStatePointer` once to the left, pointing it to the previous contact file state, and restores the contact file to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index 0, pointing to the initial ContactFile state, then there are no previous ContactFile states to restore. The `undo` command uses `Model#canUndoContactFile()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather
than attempting to perform the undo.

The `redo` command does the opposite — it calls `Model#redoContactFile()`, which shifts the `currentStatePointer` once to the right, pointing to the previously undone state, and restores the contact file to that state.

<div markdown="span" class="alert alert-info">:information_source: **Note:** If the `currentStatePointer` is at index `contactFileStateList.size() - 1`, pointing to the latest contact file state, then there are no undone ContactFile states to restore. The `redo` command uses `Model#canRedoContactFile()` to check if this is the case. If so, it will return an error to the user rather than attempting to perform the redo.

Step 5. The user then decides to execute the command `list`. Commands that do not modify the contact file, such as `list`, will usually not call `Model#commitContactFile()`, `Model#undoContactFile()` or `Model#redoContactFile()`. Thus, the `contactFileStateList` remains unchanged.

Step 6. The user executes `clear`, which calls `Model#commitContactFile()`. Since the `currentStatePointer` is not pointing at the end of the `contactFileStateList`, all contact file states after the `currentStatePointer` will be purged. Reason: It no longer makes sense to redo the `add n/David …​` command. This is the behavior that most modern desktop applications follow.

8.  Should allow only one running instance to use the contact file at a time.
9.  Should accept names containing non-English (Unicode) letters
10. Every error message should state what was wrong and, where relevant, the accepted format.

* **Contact**: A record of one person. Only the name is required; a company, a role, a contact number, an email address, a LinkedIn URL and any number of tags are each optional, and the single-valued ones hold at most one value apiece
* **Contact number**: A phone number made up of at least three digits, which may also use spaces, hyphens, a leading plus sign for a country code, and balanced parentheses
* **Prefix**: A field marker in a command, such as `c/` for a company or `e/` for an email. Prefixes are case-sensitive
* **Multi-value field**: A field that can hold several comma-separated values. Every field except the name is a multi-value field
* **Private contact detail**: A contact detail that is not meant to be shared with others
* **Normalisation**: Trimming outer spaces and collapsing repeated spaces before a value is stored or compared
* **Display value**: The normalised spelling that Astra stores and shows to the user
* **Unique key**: A contact number or email. No two contacts may share one
* **Duplicate contact**: An incoming contact whose contact number or email already belongs to an existing contact
* **Merge**: Combining the distinct values of an existing and an incoming contact into one record, keeping the existing values first
* **MSS (Main Success Scenario)**: The most common path through a use case, where everything goes as expected
* **CLI (Command Line Interface)**: A text-based interface where the user types commands instead of clicking
* **Comparison value**: The form of a value used for matching, such as the lowercase name or the digits-only contact number
* **Name-match ranking**: The eight-level order (exact full name, first, last, middle; then partial first, last, middle, full) used to sort contacts that match a name
* **Candidate list**: The numbered list of matching contacts shown when a name matches several contacts. Indices start at 1
* **Contact file**: The file that stores all contacts, at `<user-home>/.contacts-cli/contacts.jsonl`
* **JSON Lines (JSONL)**: A text format with one JSON object per line
* **Corrupted contact file**: A contact file with records that are malformed, have missing fields or invalid values, or conflict with earlier records
* **Backup file**: An unchanged copy of a corrupted contact file, saved as `contacts-corrupted-<timestamp>.jsonl`

* The project uses the `java.util.logging` package for logging.
* A class obtains a `Logger` with `LogsCenter.getLogger(Class)`, which logs messages at the configured level.
* Log messages are written to the console and a `.log` file.
* The output logging level can be controlled by changing the `LOG_LEVEL` constant in the `LogsCenter` class.
* **When choosing a level for a log message**, follow the conventions given in [_[se-edu/guides] Java: Logging conventions_](https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/logging.html).
Logic logs successful contact/preference saves and cancellations at INFO. FINE records
command classes and pending-request transitions, plus temporary-file validation and atomic
replacement in Storage. Save/permission failures and unexpected command failures are WARNINGs
with their exception causes, followed by snapshot rollback. Logic and MainWindow diagnostics
use operation/state information rather than copying complete commands or contact previews.
Existing parser/model diagnostics at finer levels can still contain user data.
Assertions check internal invariants: pending requests cannot mutate data or preferences,
rollback restores the data and filtered results, deletes remove the resolved count, and action
allocation/deletion/editing preserve monotonically allocated IDs. Input validation uses normal
exceptions and remains active when assertions are disabled.

Astra is a **desktop application for managing contacts, optimized for use through a Command Line Interface (CLI)** while retaining the benefits of a Graphical User Interface (GUI). If you type quickly, Astra can help you manage contacts faster than traditional GUI applications.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for Astra.
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar contactfile.jar`.

A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds. On first launch, Astra shows sample contacts and a welcome message. Type `clear` and then `y` to remove the sample contacts when you are ready to add your own.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `filter mode/or t/work t/friend` : Lists contacts tagged with work or friend.
* `add n/John Doe c/Acme r/Engineer p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com` : Adds a contact named `John Doe` to the Contact File.
* `delete 3`, then `y`: Deletes the 3rd contact shown in the current list.
* `followup 1 a/Send portfolio`: Records a pending action for the first displayed contact.
* `followups [overdue|today|upcoming|completed|undated]`: Reviews follow-ups across all contacts by date or status.
* `order name phone email company role tags linkedin followups interactions`: Changes the field order for every contact.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
Always launch Astra from the same home folder so it can find your saved contacts in `data/contactfile.json`.
* **No saved contact file:** Astra shows sample contacts and a welcome message explaining how to clear them.
* **Saved contacts load successfully:** The message area shows the number of loaded contacts and the full path to the contact file. A saved empty contact file stays empty.
* **Another Astra instance is using the same contact file:** Startup stops with an error. Close that instance, then launch Astra again.

If the file can be read but contains some invalid or duplicate contacts, Astra automatically keeps the valid contacts and skips the affected records. For duplicate contacts, the first valid record is kept. Recovery proceeds only if at least one valid contact remains.

An invalid saved event entry, such as `null` in a contact's `events` list, causes that entire contact to be skipped and reported. Astra does not recover individual fields or events from the damaged contact.

Before replacing the active file with the recovered contacts, Astra preserves the original file as `contactfile.original.json` and writes a `report.txt` in a separate folder under `data/recovery/`. The startup message shows how many contacts were recovered and skipped, along with the paths to the active file, backup, and report.

Read the report for the positions and reasons for skipped records in the original file. Keep the backup unchanged; use it to look up missing details, correct them, and add those contacts through Astra. Recovery is complete only when Astra displays the successful recovery message.
If the file is malformed, no valid contacts can be recovered, or recovery cannot finish safely, Astra displays **Astra startup failed** before opening the main window.

When Astra can safely preserve the original contact file, it saves `contactfile.original.json` and `report.txt` in a separate folder under `data/reports/`. The error dialog shows their paths and offers two choices:

* **Start anew:** Replaces the active contact file with an empty one and opens Astra. The startup message confirms the reset and shows the backup and report paths. Keep the backup if you want to restore contact details manually later.

* **Exit:** Closes Astra and leaves the active contact file unchanged. Closing the dialog also exits. You can repair the file or restore a known good backup while Astra is closed, then launch it again.

If Astra cannot safely prepare a reset, **Start anew** is unavailable and the contact file is not cleared. Follow the error message, check that the contact file is readable and its folder is writable, and restart after resolving the problem. If a reset fails, Astra displays an error instead of opening an empty contact file.
